hook.text: Lottery winners and accident survivors return to baseline happiness within a year.

buildup.text: Impact bias: we overestimate how long and how intensely future events will affect our emotional state.

discovery.text: Gilbert and Wilson call it affective forecasting failure. We imagine future joy or pain as permanent.

twist.text: This bias fuels bad trades. We chase promotions expecting lasting happiness and dread failures expecting lasting pain.

climax.text: Before making a fear-based or desire-based decision, remember: you'll adapt. The feeling will be shorter than you think.

punchline.text: Nothing feels as long as you think it will.

quiz.question: What does impact bias cause us to do?
options: Overestimate how long future events will affect our feelings

details.summary: Impact bias is the tendency to overestimate the intensity and duration of future emotional reactions to events. People predict that positive events will make them much happier and negative events much sadder for much longer than these events actually do.
details.whyItMatters: Impact bias drives poor decisions by inflating the anticipated emotional consequences of choices. People avoid risks whose downsides they overestimate and pursue goals whose upsides they overestimate, misallocating effort toward imagined emotional.
takeaways: People overestimate how intensely and how long future events will affect them
Immune neglect means people forget their ability to psychologically adapt
Both positive and negative events affect happiness less than expected

faq.question: Why do people overestimate future emotional impacts?
faq.answer: Focalism: people focus on the event in isolation without considering all the other things that will occupy their attention. They also underestimate their psychological immune system, which rationalizes, reframes, and adapts to both good and bad outcomes.

faq.question: How does impact bias affect major life decisions?
faq.answer: People avoid career changes because they overestimate the pain of failure, or pursue promotions because they overestimate the happiness of success. The fear of anticipated regret and the pursuit of anticipated joy both exceed what actually materializes.
